translationRepairs: Subordinate Liu Jing and Li Hanzhi fought over Luoyang; Hanzhi defeated Liu at Shenshan Temple and, pressing his advantage, moved to attack Heyang, encamping at Luokou.
Subordinate Liu Jing and Li Hanzhi fought over Luoyang; Hanzhi defeated Liu at Shengshan Temple and, pressing his advantage, moved to attack Heyang, encamping at Luokou.
The characters 聖善 are read Shengshan; the proposed spelling correctly repairs the missing final -g in Sheng.
The subordinate general Liu Jing and Li Hanzhi contested possession of Luoyang; Hanzhi defeated Jing at Shenshan Temple; seizing victory, he wished to attack Heyang and encamped at Luokou.
The subordinate general Liu Jing and Li Hanzhi contested possession of Luoyang; Hanzhi defeated Jing at Shengshan Temple; seizing victory, he wished to attack Heyang and encamped at Luokou.
The literal field contains the same romanization error: 聖善寺 is Shengshan Temple, not Shenshan Temple.

(《Old Tales of Luoyang Gentry》: Whenever the Prince was pleased with a household's farming and weaving, if some family that year had good silkworms and wheat within one li of the capital, he would certainly ride there on horseback, summon all the old and young of that family, personally comfort and encourage them, and bestow wine, food, tea, and colored goods; to the men he gave cloth trousers, to the women skirts and jackets; at the time the common people still favored blue clothing, and the women all had theirs made of blue silk.

(《Old Tales of Luoyang Gentry》: Whenever the Prince was pleased with a household's farming and weaving, if some family that year had good silkworms and wheat within one she (a day's journey) of the capital, he would certainly ride there on horseback, summon all the old and young of that family, personally comfort and encourage them, and bestow wine, food, tea, and colored goods; to the men he gave cloth trousers, to the women skirts and jackets; at the time the common people still favored blue clothing, and the women all had theirs made of blue silk.
舍 denotes a travel stage, conventionally a day's journey, so translating 一舍 as one li materially understates the distance.
The Founder of Liang forced Emperor Zhaozong to move east and ordered Quanyi to repair the Luoyang palace city; only after many years was it gathered together.
The Founder of Liang forced Emperor Zhaozong to move east and ordered Quanyi to repair the Luoyang palace city; only after many years was it completed.
In this construction, 累年方集 says that the repair project was completed only after several years; 'gathered together' is not idiomatic or accurate here.

(《Old Tales of Luoyang Gentry》 notes that the Prince of Qi and the Liang Founder had both served as central secretariat ministers; when the Founder took four commands concurrently, the Prince repeatedly asked to yield his concurrent posts, having sensed the Founder's ambition and seeking to keep himself safe.

(《Old Tales of Luoyang Gentry》 notes that the Prince of Qi and the Liang Founder had each served as Minister of the Central Secretariat and Minister of the Imperial Secretariat; when the Founder took four commands concurrently, the Prince repeatedly asked to yield his concurrent posts, having sensed the Founder's ambition and seeking to keep himself safe.
中書令 and 尚書令 are distinct offices, and the proposal correctly restores both rather than collapsing them into a vague single designation.
When, after the Founder of Liang lost his army in Hebei and Shuo, each month he presented armor and horses to replenish his forces;
After the Founder of Liang lost an army in Hebei, Quanyi presented armor and horses each month to replenish his forces;
Removing the ungrammatical opening is necessary, but the proposal leaves 'he' ambiguous between Quanyi and the Founder. The revision names Quanyi as the silent subject of 月獻.
Quanyi's wife was the Chu clan; she was bright, keen, and had stratagems.
Quanyi's wife was Lady Chu; she was bright, keen, and had stratagems.
儲氏 identifies a woman by surname and is correctly rendered 'Lady Chu'; saying that the wife 'was the Chu clan' is erroneous English.

(《Unofficial Biography of the Prince of Qi》 records that the Founder suspected the Prince and tried four times to kill him; Lady Chu pleaded with him in person and saved her husband; the Founder then had his son the Prince of Fu marry the Prince of Qi's daughter.)〉

(The Unofficial Biography of the Prince of Qi records that the Founder suspected the Prince and tried four times to kill him; Lady Chu pleaded with him in person and saved her husband; the Founder then had his son the Prince of Fu marry the Prince of Qi's daughter.)
The replacement cleanly renders the enclosing Chinese note and title punctuation in English and removes the unmatched closing annotation mark.
The emperor comforted him at length, had attendants help the old man up the hall, feasted him generously, and ordered Prince Jiji, Prince Cunji, and others to treat him as an elder brother.

The emperor comforted him at length, had attendants help the old man up the hall, feasted him generously, and ordered his son Jiji, his younger brother Cunji, and the others to treat him as an elder brother.
皇子 and 皇弟 specify the emperor's son and younger brother, not princely titles. The revision preserves those relationships in natural idiomatic English.

Quanyi stopped him, saying, "At Heyang I once endured Li Hanzhi's siege for a year, eating wood shavings day to day and expecting death at any moment until another saved me and brought me to today—that debt cannot be repaid with betrayal."

Quanyi stopped him, saying, "When I was at Heyang, Li Hanzhi brought the Taiyuan army to besiege me for a full year. I survived from day to day on wood shavings and expected death at any moment, until another came to my rescue and brought me to where I am today. I cannot betray that kindness."
The proposal restores the Taiyuan army and 恩, but 'met Li Hanzhi's calamity' is not idiomatic. The revision conveys the siege, privation, rescue, and obligation without that distortion.
He later entered the service of Wang Hong, military governor of Shanzhou, and rose by merit to regimental commander.
He later entered the service of Wang Gong, military governor of Shanzhou, and rose by merit to regimental commander.
The name 王珙 is Wang Gong; 'Wang Hong' misreads the character 珙 and must be corrected in the idiomatic field.
Later he served the Shanzhou military governor Wang Hong and through accumulated merit reached army commander.
Later he served the Shanzhou military governor Wang Gong and through accumulated merit reached army commander.
The name 王珙 is Wang Gong; the same incorrect 'Wang Hong' romanization must be repaired in the literal field.
Wang Hong was harsh and graceless toward his men; Li Fan, a favored staff officer, bore the brunt of his rage at the slightest offense and secretly nursed a grudge.
Wang Gong was harsh and graceless toward his men; Li Fan, a favored staff officer, bore the brunt of his rage at the slightest offense and secretly nursed a grudge.
The abbreviated 珙 still refers to Wang Gong, so the proposed idiomatic name correction is required and complete.
Wang Hong was harsh and graceless toward his men; Li Fan, a favored staff officer, bore the brunt of his rage at the slightest offense and secretly nursed a grudge.
Wang Gong was harsh and graceless toward his men; Li Fan, a favored staff officer, bore the brunt of his rage at the slightest offense and secretly nursed a grudge.
The abbreviated 珙 still refers to Wang Gong, so the literal field must likewise replace the erroneous name Wang Hong.
In 898 Wang Hong and his brother Ke, military governor of Hezhong, fell into open war; Hong's armies kept losing and his troops lost heart.
In 898 Wang Gong and his brother Ke, military governor of Hezhong, fell into open war; Gong's armies kept losing and his troops lost heart.
Both occurrences of 珙 designate Gong, and the proposal correctly repairs Wang Hong and the shortened Hong in the idiomatic sentence.

In the first year of Guanghua, Hong and his younger brother the Hezhong military governor Ke confronted each other; arms were sought day by day; Hong's troops repeatedly were defeated; the ranks lost heart.

In the first year of Guanghua, Gong and his younger brother the Hezhong military governor Ke confronted each other; arms were sought day by day; Gong's troops repeatedly were defeated; the ranks lost heart.
Both instances of 珙 are Gong, so replacing Hong with Gong in the literal sentence is correct.
In the sixth month of the following year Fan killed Hong, went over to the Liang, and the Liang Founder had him appointed military governor of Shanzhou.
In the sixth month of the following year Fan killed Gong, went over to the Liang, and the Liang Founder had him appointed military governor of Shanzhou.
The object of 璠殺珙 is Wang Gong, so the idiomatic sentence correctly changes Hong to Gong.
In the sixth month of the second year Fan killed Hong, submitted to the Bian men, and the Founder of Liang memorialized Fan as military governor of Shanzhou.
In the sixth month of the second year Fan killed Gong, submitted to the Bian men, and the Founder of Liang memorialized Fan as military governor of Shanzhou.
The object of 璠殺珙 is Wang Gong, so the same Hong-to-Gong correction is required in the literal sentence.

The Luoyang army supervisor once obtained the sobering stone from Director Li's Pingquan estate; Quanyi sought it; the supervisor would not give it; Quanyi immediately killed him—his clinging to power and making might were again thus.

The Luoyang army supervisor once obtained the sobering stone from Grand Commandant Li's Pingquan estate; Quanyi sought it; the supervisor would not give it; Quanyi immediately killed him—his clinging to power and making might were again thus.
太尉 is the office Grand Commandant; 'Director Li' mistranslates the title attached to Li Deyu.
Youqian said: "The Prince of Jin personally rushed to my urgency, at midnight bore candles to fight the enemy, face to face made covenant oath, and will not betray the first heart.
Youqian said: "The Prince of Jin personally came to my aid, fought the enemy by torchlight at midnight, made a covenant with me face to face, and has not betrayed his original commitment.
The grammatical subject naturally remains the Prince of Jin through 不負初心; the Chinese does not mark a switch to Youqian as 'I.' The revision clarifies the continuing subject and tense.

Yesterday I heard of my reporting difficulty; he ordered the general to march by starlight, aided my provisions and grain, divided my clothes and shoes—yet you wish to turn over and betray grace; this is what is called Duke Qi of Deng's saying, 'Men will not eat what I leave over.'

Only recently, upon hearing my appeal for aid, he ordered his generals to march by starlight, supplied me with provisions, and shared his clothing and footwear with me; yet you would reverse course and betray his kindness. This is what Duke Qi of Deng meant when he said, 'Men will not eat what I leave behind.'"
The proposal correctly restores the Prince as hearer and donor, but 'When recently' and 'turn and betray that grace' are awkward. The revision keeps each subject and object explicit.

Emperor Zhuangzong set a feast to feast and comfort him, favor and gifts without reckoning; he personally poured the goblet and entrusted Youqian, saying: "He who completed my great enterprise—you, sir, are the force."

Emperor Zhuangzong held a banquet to entertain and reward him, bestowing favors and gifts beyond reckoning; he personally poured a cup and offered it to Youqian, saying: "It was through your strength, sir, that I accomplished my great enterprise."
屬 here means offering or urging a cup, not entrusting someone. The revision makes that action explicit and removes the proposal's remaining 'set a feast to feast' tautology.
His sons Lingde and Lingxi were made military governors of Suizhou and Xuzhou.
His sons Lingde and Lingxi were made military governors of Suizhou and Xu Prefecture.
許州 is Xu Prefecture, distinct from Xuzhou written 徐州; the proposed wording removes the misleading homophony.
(According to Wu Zhen's Errors of Usurpation, the Biography of Shi Yanqiong records that Youqian's son Jianhui was killed,
(According to Wu Zhen's Compendium of Errors (Zuanwu), the Biography of Shi Yanqiong records that Youqian's son Jianhui was killed,

The cited work is Wu Zhen's 五代史纂誤, not 'Errors of Usurpation.' 'Compendium of Errors' more closely renders 纂誤 than the proposal's 'Corrections of Errors.'
he ordered Jiji to execute Lingde at Suizhou and Wang Sitong to execute Lingxi at Xuzhou,
he ordered Jiji to execute Lingde at Suizhou and Wang Sitong to execute Lingxi at Xu Prefecture,
The place is 許州, Xu Prefecture, not Xuzhou 徐州; the proposed idiomatic replacement correctly distinguishes them.
he decreed that Jiji execute Lingde at Suizhou and Wang Sitong execute Lingxi at Xuzhou,
he decreed that Jiji execute Lingde at Suizhou and Wang Sitong execute Lingxi at Xu Prefecture,
The place is 許州, Xu Prefecture, not Xuzhou 徐州; the same distinction is required in the literal field.
